biography.plain_text: Bernard Madoff was an American financier who founded a New York securities firm, helped by his father-in-law’s early client introductions. His investment fraud enriched him by diverting clients’ money. In 2009, he pleaded guilty to eleven federal felonies arising from a vast Ponzi scheme and received a 150-year prison sentence.

long_biography.plain_text:
Bernard Madoff’s securities firm helped establish electronic share trading, while its investment advisory business concealed a vast fraud. He served as Nasdaq chairman in the early 1990s. The firm’s market-making operation bought and sold securities to other brokers, earning the difference between its buying and selling prices. Advisory clients, meanwhile, received fabricated records of investments that had never been made.

When withdrawal demands mounted during the financial crisis in 2008, Madoff could no longer sustain the deception. He confessed to his sons, whose lawyer alerted the authorities. Criminal proceedings stripped him of his property, including his investments and homes. He died in federal custody in 2021.

Quantitative investing would falsely imply the advertised strategy was performed; Investment banking does not describe the brokerage.
